@@129899378 <p> Filmmaker Raoul Peck uses George Orwell 's writings to weave together a biographical portrait of the author and a dispiriting picture of power and truth in the modern world in " Orwell : 2+2=5 . " <p> He 's hardly the first to connect the dots between Orwell 's prophetic writings and the current state of things -- remember , sales for " Nineteen Eighty-Four " soared in the months following Donald Trump 's first election when phrases like " alternative facts " were being used with no irony . Knowing that , Peck draws heavily on what has come before . The film is packed with clips from film adaptations of " 1984 , " including Michael Anderson 's black and white version from 1956 , and Michael Radford 's , released in 1984 , documentaries , like Robert Kane Pappas 's 2003 warning " Orwell Rolls in His Grave , " and news footage from World War II through Gaza . In sum , it makes a persuasive point that things are only getting worse . <p> " Orwell : 2+2=5 " is loosely structured around Orwell @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , where he wrote what would be his last novel , " 1984 , " while his health was deteriorating from tuberculosis . He went to Jura in 1946 and was dead by 1950 . But this is no Wikipedia page or college lecture . There are no talking heads and no one explaining , " War is peace . Freedom is slavery . Ignorance is strength . " <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> Instead , it 's a loose assembly of biography , reflection and key moments of political awakening , with actor Damian Lewis narrating Orwell 's words with a poetic gravitas , interspersed with a collage of images , words and archival footage . Anything from David Lean 's " Oliver Twist " and Sydney Pollack " Out of Africa " to Lauren Greenfield 's " Generation Wealth " is on the table , and nothing is there carelessly . Alexei Aigui 's powerful score adds a melancholy weight to sequences showing wartime destruction past and present along with the political phrases used to describe them : A " strategic bombing " in Berlin in 1945 , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ clearance operation " in Myanmar in 2017 . <p> There 's a purposefully disorienting effect to the film 's editing , blending past , present , fiction and reality in such a way that it all begins to blur together . By the time we 're hearing Lewis utter Orwell 's famous phrase " the very concept of objective truth is fading out of the world " while AI images pollute the screen , it 's easy to forget that the quote is seven decades old . It wo n't prepare you for any kind of historical report on Orwell , totalitarianism or doublespeak , but its impact is undeniable . <p> Orwell understood that every writer is a product of their own time . Born Eric Arthur Blair in Motihari , Bihar , then an outpost of the British Empire , Peck focuses in on a photograph of him as a baby with his Indian nursemaid . Describing himself as " lower upper middle class , " Orwell attended Eton and served with the British Imperial Police in Burma ( now Myanmar ) and observed how power manifested in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ accessible to any white man simply because they were white . He considered himself both a snob and a revolutionary , which only intensified as he picked up more life experiences through the Spanish Civil War , his time at the BBC and simply observing ordinary people around him . It 's actually quite extraordinary just how much information Peck , who has delved into the lives of James Baldwin , Karl Marx , Patrice Lumumba and Ernest Cole , is able to convey in just under two hours . <p> " Orwell : 2+2=5 " might not be as fully realized as Peck 's 2017 knockout " I Am Not Your Negro , " but it is no less essential . It hardly matters that Orwell is on every high schooler 's syllabus , that doublespeak and big brother are household phrases , or that every few years there is some film , some book , some article reminding us of his big ideas . Earlier this year Andy Serkis even debuted a new animated version of " Animal Farm " at a film festival . <p> Orwell died @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ know just how prophetic his work would become . While every writer dreams of their words , their thoughts living on , would n't it be nice if , for a moment , these were n't so awfully relevant ? <p> " Orwell : 2+2=5 , " a Neon release in select theaters Friday , has not been rated by the Motion Picture Association . Running time : 119 minutes . @@129982360 <h> Local Vinnies president addresses Examiner editorial on landfill fees <p> A recent editorial suggests that charitable thrift stores like Vinnies must survive without landfill subsidies , invoking the " rule of the market " as the ultimate test of viability . While concerns about waste management and efficiency are valid , the underlying assumption -- that government should operate like a business -- is deeply flawed . <p> Governments exist not to maximize profit , but to serve the public good . That includes supporting organizations whose mission is to uplift the vulnerable -- those who rely on food banks , affordable goods and community care . <p> Vinnies , run by The Society of St. Vincent de Paul ( Peterborough ) , has long been a pillar of support in Peterborough and Lakefield . Its thrift stores generate revenue that directly funds food security and emergency assistance . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> The editorial notes a landfill fee exemption worth nearly $300,000 over four years . While substantial , this figure is modest compared to the social value returned . Framing it as a " sweet deal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Yes , Vinnies must address unsellable donations and after-hours dumping . Responsible stewardship matters . But to suggest its future should be dictated solely by market forces ignores why such organizations exist : to serve where the market fails . <p> Unlike corporate chains like Value Village -- whose profits flow to multinational investors -- Vinnies operates with purpose , not profit . Its mission is rooted in dignity , faith and service . Equating it with commercial enterprises overlooks the true role of charity in civic life . <p> Every dollar raised by Vinnies supports vital programs , including its food bank . These funds stay local -- supporting wages , sustaining jobs and circulating through nearby businesses . Vinnies strengthens both the social fabric and the local economy in ways no corporate model can replicate . <p> Governments at all levels have a duty to represent all citizens -- not just the economically productive , but also the marginalized , the elderly and the poor . When budgets tighten , it 's tempting to cut support for those who ca n't push back . But that is precisely @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ moral obligation . <p> This debate is n't just about garbage -- it 's about values and whether we believe communities thrive through compassion or competition . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> Peter Gruneberg , president of The Society of St Vincent de Paul in Peterborough <h> Vinnies opinion uninformed <p> You make statements such as " Vinnies brought some of this on itself " and " There are other thrift stores and other food banks people can use . " <p> Before making such statements , a " journalist " would have done their due diligence and visited all food banks in the city and accurately compared the services offered . A " journalist " would have investigated the need that Vinnies addresses in this community and the system failure that created this need . <p> I invite you to go line up with Vinnies ' clients , talk to them , ask them if " other " food banks will be just fine for them . Ask them what they will do if Vinnies was no longer in the picture . <p> The food @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are humans with needs that a small army of volunteers at Vinnies selflessly serves . <p> Vinnies is not Value Village . The profit Vinnies makes buys tuna cans , bean cans , bread , ground beef , milk and eggs to hand out to the families who depend on it to survive . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> Until you have visited all Peterborough 's food banks , collected the facts and talked to the food bank users , you have no right to make such statements . <p> Words matter . @@130040825 <h> Treasure Trove : These dog tags are a poignant reminder of the hostages in Gaza <p> This is the first Treasure Trove that features an item I wear every day . <p> Like all of us who wear the hostage dog tags , I look forward to the day when I can take it off as that would mean the hostages are finally home . <p> They are modelled on the dog tags soldiers wear , a practice that started during the American Civil War when soldiers were worried that they would not be identified after they were killed and would be buried in unmarked graves . Soldiers who could afford them , purchased engraved metal tags from private vendors to ensure this did not happen to them . It was only in 1906 that the United States Army required that ID tags be worn by its soldiers . <p> The Hebrew text of the hostage dog tags ( halev shelanu shavui b'Aza ) means " our heart is captive in Gaza . " Notice that the word " heart " is singular and not plural . The idea @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ moment we first became a nation at Mount Sinai . Rashi noted that when the Jewish people arrived at Mount Sinai they encamped like one person with one heart -- in other words , they were united . <p> Whether the Jewish people share one heart in working for the return of the hostages is a question that history will judge . But our people are not complete , and our heart will remain broken , until all of the hostages ( living and dead ) are brought home . <p> The yellow ribbon is also a cry for the return of the hostages . Its origin is much more pedestrian than the Torah or United States military history . The yellow ribbon as a symbol of hostage return started with the U.S. diplomats held hostage in Iran in 1979 . <p> Penne Laingen , the wife of Bruce Laingen who was one of the hostages , was asked what Americans can do to help the hostages . She thought that demonstrations of violence and anger would not help free them , so she said , " Tell them to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of patience . Just tell them to tie a yellow ribbon around the old oak tree . " <p> Laingen was referring to this 1973 song by Tony Orlando and Dawn . It tells the story of a man released from prison who wondered whether his love wants him back , and if she does , she should tie a yellow ribbon on a certain tree to let him know . If he does n't see it when his bus rolls into town , he will know she does n't want him and will stay on the bus . Happily , she ties 100 yellow ribbons on the tree and everyone on the bus cheers for him . He says " I 'm coming home . " <p> We wait for the day that all of the hostages are home , the yellow ribbons can be put away and the dog tags can be taken off . It is then that the work of healing and repair can really begin . One day in captivity is too long . On Oct. 5 , it will be 730 days . Since the start of 2025 , steep new tariffs imposed on goods coming into the U.S. have strained businesses and consumers alike , pushing costs higher and weakening the job market . Hiring has dropped while inflation continues to inch upward . Consumer pessimism is growing . <p> The current U.S. government shutdown has added to those anxieties . " <p> When a bad man does a good thing , we should honour him for it even if his motives are selfish . <p> Donald Trump is only trying to " bring peace to the Middle East " because he wants the Nobel Prize , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ He boasts about the seven wars he claims to have settled/ended/avoided , but he can not even tell the difference between Armenia ( which did recently have a war ) and Albania ( which did n't ) . <p> All true , but so what ? @@130237447 <p> Ya'ara Saks during her visit to the West Bank March 15 , 2024 ( photo via Instagram ) <p> Oct. 7 , 2023 , was a day that changed Israel -- and Jewish communities across the world -- forever . The murder of more than 1,200 people and the kidnapping of hundreds more by Hamas terrorists marked not only the worst massacre of Jews since the Holocaust , but the beginning of a tragedy that has since displaced over 1.5 million Palestinians , forced nearly 100,000 Israelis from their homes , and left tens of thousands grieving on both sides . <p> In the two years since , grief and anger have filled every corner of Jewish life . Yet out of this devastation , one truth has become painfully clear : there is no alternative to peace . The cost of abandoning a two-state solution is too high , and the moral and human consequences are intolerable . <p> Canada , for decades , has stood firm in its support for two states for two peoples -- a policy rooted in diplomacy , compassion , and justice . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that Israel 's long-term security is inseparable from Palestinian self-determination . While the region and its politics have shifted , the vision must remain constant : a sovereign Israel living in security alongside a sovereign Palestine built on dignity and equality . <p> Disarming Hamas is not enough . The terror organization that launched the barbaric attack of October 7 can have no place in whatever comes next . Israelis must know they are safe and secure . Palestinians must have the agency to demand leadership that is committed to a collaborative path -- one that builds governance for the people they serve , not vengeance or victory , but safety , stability , and normalized relations . <p> As fragile as it is , the most recent agreement between Israel and Hamas has once again placed both peoples in a tense waiting game . Hostages may soon come home . Violence may slow . Humanitarian aid may finally reach Gazans who have endured unimaginable suffering . Israelis and Palestinians alike are waiting to exhale -- to imagine , perhaps for the first time in years , what " normal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . It demands leadership willing to risk political consequence for moral clarity . I know this from experience . <p> During the height of the war , I travelled to Ramallah -- not because it was politically convenient , and certainly not because it was easy as a Canadian-Israeli and a cabinet minister -- but because it was necessary . That meeting was one of the few quiet steps that helped build a foundation for the difficult conversation that continues today : what conditions must the Palestinian Authority meet to open a genuine path forward ? <p> Those conditions are not new . They include transparent elections , an end to corruption , the dismantling of the welfare system that rewards terror , and the rebuilding of a generation through education for reconciliation and mutual recognition -- not violence . These are the steps that make peace possible . <p> Hope , I have learned , is not na ? ve . It is strategic . It is an act of defiance in the face of adversity . Hope is how we persevere through despair , how we shape policy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ we remind ourselves that courage does not come from certainty , but from conviction . <p> Leadership and agency must also come from within . Hamas has led the Palestinian people into ruin . Their unrelenting pursuit of violent resistance -- at the cost of their own citizens ' lives -- has turned Gaza into a place of devastation and despair . For Palestinians to have a future , their national movement must reject Hamas 's ideology of annihilation . The Palestinian people deserve leaders who understand that a viable , independent state can only exist alongside a safe and secure Israel . <p> This truth lies at the heart of the matter . If we are to rebuild trust and establish a lasting peace , Israelis and Palestinians alike must confront a simple , uncomfortable reality : our lives are intertwined . Our safety depends on one another . <p> For Jewish communities here in Canada , this truth carries a parallel responsibility . We have lived through two years of fear , mourning , and rising antisemitism . Many of us have felt isolated in our grief and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , we can not lose sight of our values -- the belief that peace , security , and justice are not mutually exclusive but mutually dependent . <p> We are tired , yes -- but we are not broken . <p> This moment , fragile as it is , offers an opening . It calls for moral courage -- not only from leaders in the region but from allies like Canada who can help nurture reconciliation , rebuild institutions , and ensure accountability . Canada must be part of that work . <p> It is not enough to stand with Israel in solidarity ; we must also stand with Israelis and Palestinians who are willing to build a different future . Peace is not inevitable , but it is possible -- if we insist on it . <p> As our sages taught : " Lo alecha hamelacha ligmor , v'lo atah ben chorin l'hibatel mimena " -- " It is not upon you to complete the work , but neither are you free to desist from it . " <p> That teaching has guided the Jewish people through millennia of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ We can not complete the work of peace -- but we must never stop trying . <p> Ya'ara Saks is the former Member of Parliament for York Centre and the former Minister of Mental Health and Addictions , and Associate Minister of Health . <h> Author <h> Support Our Mission : Make a Difference ! <p> The Canadian Jewish News is now a Registered Journalism Organization ( RJO ) as defined by the Canada Revenue Agency . Gift this article to friends and family for free . <p> Samer Sinijlawi is a political activist and a Palestinian political @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and Instagram ssinijlawi <p> As the devastating war in Gaza rages on , Palestinians find themselves confronting not only destruction and loss but also a profound absence of leadership . The official Palestinian establishment , embodied by President Mahmoud Abbas , has failed to meet the historic gravity of this moment . With a fragile ceasefire now in place , the urgency is no longer only about ending the fighting -- it is about shaping what comes next . The days after the guns fall silent will demand credible , unified , and strategic leadership capable of guiding Gaza 's recovery and the nation 's political renewal . <p> At a time when the Palestinian cause commands unprecedented global attention , this recognition is not the product of purposeful diplomacy but the consequence of human tragedy . The world 's conscience has been stirred not by strategy , but by the haunting images of suffering broadcast daily from Gaza . That attention , however , will soon shift unless it is matched by Palestinian leadership ready to channel global sympathy into a coherent plan for peace and reconstruction . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ administering Gaza after the war , serious doubts persist about its capacity and credibility . Public trust in the leadership has eroded dramatically , and the absence of a coherent strategy or active diplomacy underscores a deep vacuum at the heart of Palestinian politics . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> President Abbas , increasingly disconnected from the Palestinian street , commands neither popular support nor the political vitality required to effect meaningful change . His annual addresses at the UN General Assembly have become rituals devoid of substance -- gestures of a leadership that long ago lost touch with the aspirations of its people . <p> Palestinians are exhausted by years of paralysis and disillusionment . What they need now is not bureaucratic continuity but moral and political renewal -- leaders who act decisively in pursuit of justice , freedom , and national dignity . <p> At the center of that renewal must be free and fair presidential and legislative elections . President Abbas himself pledged in a letter dated June 8 , 2025 , to Saudi Arabia 's Crown Prince and the President of France @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " national and constitutional entitlement . " That promise must no longer be deferred . <p> Elections should take place as soon as the basic necessities of life are restored in Gaza -- when people have shelter , water , electricity , and the minimum stability required to vote freely and safely . They must follow , but not wait indefinitely behind , the early stages of the ceasefire 's implementation . The process of national renewal can not be postponed until " everything is ready , " because political legitimacy is itself a cornerstone of recovery . <p> Palestinians must be allowed to choose their government for themselves -- in Gaza , the West Bank , and East Jerusalem alike . Only a leadership born from the people 's will can credibly represent them in rebuilding their homeland and engaging the world . Elections are not a luxury ; they are an urgent necessity to restore legitimacy , rebuild trust , and create the conditions for real change . Above all , they are the indispensable gateway to ending the suffering of our people in Gaza . <p> Still @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ change are not limited to the absence of charismatic leadership . They also lie in entrenched interests , the structural violence of occupation , the manipulation of narratives , and the inertia of international diplomacy . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> If there is a lesson to draw from history -- and from the vision of those Palestinians who still believe in coexistence -- it is that human dignity , equal citizenship , and pragmatic institutional reform offer far more durable paths to justice than the search for a singular savior . <p> Canada , France , and the United Kingdom announced last month their recognition of a Palestinian state . But recognition without reconciliation risks becoming mere theater . Too often , Palestinian leaders have celebrated symbolic gestures by countries thousands of miles away while neglecting the one relationship that truly determines the fate of Palestinian sovereignty : the relationship with Israel . <p> Real peace requires strategy , not symbolism . It requires dialogue with Israelis -- not just speeches before the G7 or the UN . It demands less energy spent on hollow @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and alliances with the only state that can make a Palestinian state a reality . <p> The recent ceasefire agreement , brokered through unprecedented international coordination , offers a fragile but vital opportunity . It must mark not an end point , but a beginning -- a moment to translate humanitarian relief into political momentum and moral responsibility . <p> Until we convince Israelis that Palestinian independence serves their own security and future , nothing fundamental will change on the ground . Diplomatic missions across the world will not bring peace to the Middle East . Honest conversations in Israeli neighborhoods just might . <p> But while these steps are historic , the hard work now begins -- turning promises into realities , and ensuring that rebuilding does not stop at concrete and steel but extends to trust and coexistence . <p> Opinion Headlines Newsletter <p> Take a stand with this regular roundup of the best from our columnists . <p> Error ! It will face an uphill battle to end the political crisis <p> PARIS ( AP ) -- France 's newly reappointed Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu named a new government Sunday , as he faces pressure to urgently produce a budget and quell political turmoil that is scaring businesses and investors and staining the country 's image . <p> The Cabinet includes several familiar faces from previous governments who hail from French President Emmanuel Macron 's centrist camp as well as allied conservatives , and some people from outside the political sphere . <p> Immediately after the president 's office announced the new Cabinet , the conservative Republicans party announced it was expelling the six party members who agreed to join the government . <p> Lecornu , a 39-year-old centrist and close ally of Macron , and his government will now have to seek compromises to avoid an immediate vote of no confidence in the National Assembly , deeply fractured among far right , centrist and left-wing camps . <p> Among new appointments is a new defense minister , former Labor @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ support for Ukraine and address threats to European security posed by Russia . <p> Paris police chief Laurent Nunez , who oversaw security for the 2024 Olympics , becomes interior minister , in charge of national security . Roland Lescure will be finance minister , a crucial job as France tries to produce a budget that tackles ballooning debt and growing poverty . <p> Those keeping their jobs include Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot , who travels Monday with Macron to Egypt for an international ceremony marking the Gaza ceasefire . <p> Lecornu , France 's fourth prime minister in a year , appointed his first government a week ago -- then resigned hours later amid protests by a key conservative coalition member . That unleashed days of political uncertainty . <p> Macron persuaded Lecornu to stay on as prime minister and renamed him Friday . Lecornu acknowledged Saturday that there were n't " a lot of candidates " for his job -- and that he might not last long in the post given the country 's deep political divides . <p> Lecornu may be forced to abandon an unpopular pension @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ his second presidential term . Rammed through parliament without a vote in 2023 despite mass protests , it gradually raises the retirement age from 62 to 64 . Opposition parties want it scrapped . <p> Macron 's shock decision last year to dissolve the National Assembly produced a hung parliament and political paralysis as it faces a debt crisis that has worried domestic businesses , global financial markets and EU partners .

@@130337591 <p> For the last two years , when Israelis or diaspora Jews would talk about bringing the last living hostages home , there was a belief their spoken words would never betray : the hostages would not come home . Not all of them . Not all at once . <p> The hostages were too valuable to Hamas , serving as their only real bargaining chip in a war that the Israeli Defense Forces ( IDF ) will win on strength , military intelligence and strategy every time . In 2011 , Israel exchanged 1,027 prisoners for Gilad Shalit , an Israeli soldier captured by Hamas and held in captivity for five years . So what concessions could Hamas extract holding onto a handful now ? <p> But on Monday , what was once unthinkable actually happened : all 20 of the last living Israeli hostages were returned home . And in exchange , Hamas got an end to Israel 's bombing campaign and the release of nearly 2,000 Palestinian prisoners . It did not , notably , secure the withdrawal of the IDF which , for now , still @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ How ? And why now ? What convinced Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to sign onto a peace deal where the " day-after " plan -- of demilitarization of the Gaza Strip , of the destruction of Hamas 's terror tunnels , of transitional government by Palestinian technocrats -- is hardly guaranteed , particularly with the professed goal of " destroying Hamas " yet incomplete ? And why would Hamas agree to a ceasefire deal where they give up all their hostages at once , agree to forfeit their weapons , their infrastructure and their power , and only then see the IDF withdraw completely from Gaza ? <p> The necessary element was Donald Trump . The U.S. President is running his administration like a despotic regime , but in this one specific case , he really was the broker of peace . The first phase of this ceasefire simply could not have happened without him . <p> Israeli columnist Gershon Baskin , who was involved in negotiations during Joe Biden 's time in the White House , said recently that a nearly identical deal was put on the table @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of Israeli hostages , more of whom were alive at the time ) , but it was rejected by Mr. Netanyahu . According to Mr. Baskin , the Israelis were waiting for a change in U.S. administration before they would consider terms for a permanent ceasefire . <p> The geopolitical situation in the Middle East has changed since then ; Hamas is isolated from its regional allies in Lebanon , Yemen and Iran , who have been weakened by Israeli attacks . Mr. Netanyahu was also facing ever-intensifying internal pressure to end the war and finally bring the hostages home . But Mr. Trump was the necessary element to get it done . <p> Mr. Trump offers something of an intangible guarantee ; his support for Israel has been unwavering , even as allies , including Canada , lined up to declare their recognition of a Palestinian state . And unlike Mr. Biden , who entertained the prospect of an arms embargo , Mr. Trump has actually fast-tracked arms deliveries to Israel . When Israelis say that Mr. Trump is the " best friend " they have ever had in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ would not trust another President to implement this kind of deal . <p> This is meaningful to Hamas , too , which has seen that Mr. Trump 's close personal relationship with Mr. Netanyahu has also been leveraged to apply pressure on the Israeli Prime Minister , who made a call at Mr. Trump 's behest to the Qatari Prime Minister to apologize for his failed strike in Doha in early September . That offers some assurances to Hamas that Mr. Trump will force the Israelis to stick to their terms of the deal , though certainly the co-ordinated pressure from regional players -- Egypt , Qatar and Turkey , as orchestrated by the White House -- was instrumental in getting Hamas to sign onto the ceasefire . <p> But that was n't all : there 's a compelling factor in Mr. Trump himself -- his unpredictability , erraticism , his willingness to cross red lines . Mr. Trump wanted a peace deal , and he warned that " all hell " would break out against Hamas if the group did not agree to " this last-chance agreement . " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ; Mr. Trump sent B2 stealth fighters to aid in Israel 's military operation in Iran in June , after all . What would he do in Gaza ? <p> Mr. Trump was the essential element that got the first phase of this peace deal done . The rest is hardly guaranteed ( indeed , an easily bored President who is more interested in adoring headlines than enduring hard work could soon lose interest in the deal altogether ) , but he nevertheless succeeded in ending the bombing , and bringing the last living hostages home . Loathe him as one might for his cacophony of destructive and chaotic behaviours , on this essential step toward Middle East peace , Donald Trump got it done .

@@130373437 <h> Sections <h> Links <h> Point of Inquiry : Is stability worth a restriction on autonomy ? The AMS asks students to decide for resource groups . <p> At the upcoming AGM , the AMS is going to ask members to support bylaw amendments that give long-term stability to resource groups like the Social Justice Centre and Pride Collective -- at the cost of some autonomy , writes AMS Columnist Quyen Schroeder . <p> Point of Inquiry is a column written by AMS Columnist Quyen Schroeder about our student union 's governance and policies . It seeks to analyze the AMS with a critical -- but constructive -- eye . <p> Quyen Schroeder ( they/she ) is a fourth-year student studying English language and computer science , and they 've been a committed observer of almost all AMS Council meetings since February 2023 . She also ran as " Barry ' Bee ' Buzzword " in the 2025 AMS Presidential election . They can be reached atq.schroeder@ubyssey.ca . <p> Bylaw changes are coming -- and you 'll be able to vote for them on Oct. 22 at the AMS ' @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Bylaws are the union 's most stable governing document . To change them , the union must call a general meeting or propose a referendum item . Then , two-thirds of voters must vote in favour of the change . <p> During a general election , for a bylaw change to be quorate -- that is , for enough students to vote in it for it to count -- eight per cent of UBC 's student body needs to vote . For next week 's AGM , that number is one per cent of students : just over 600 people . By showing up on Oct. 22 , your vote for or against these bylaw changes will be significantly more impactful . <p> I 'll break down these changes so you can decide whether it 's worth turning out to the AGM to support these bylaws or just for the chance at a year-long supply of Blue Chip cookies . While I think you should show up to the AGM , these bylaw changes are unlikely to affect any individual student directly . For the AMS 's resource groups , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the union and the campus community at large . <p> Most of the bylaw changes are minor , representing clarifications on the duties of AMS executives and small tweaks to wording that align the bylaws with provincial legislation . <h> Filling vacancies <p> These bylaw changes allow the AMS to create procedures to deem a seat vacant and to appoint temporary replacements for vacant members . Multiple voting seats on council are currently vacant . The creation of a procedure to fill these seats on an interim basis is beneficial . The Affiliate Colleges ( which includes Corpus Christi , Saint Mark 's College , Regent College and Vancouver School of Theology ) and the Graduate Student Society often struggle to fill seats . A process for appointing members to vacant seats has limited effectiveness without those willing to serve . <p> I 'm somewhat concerned about the potential of this to be used to avoid elections and appoint ideologically complacent replacements . In recent years , AMS executives who ' left ' the AMS have taken an indefinite leave of absence without technically resigning . As such , the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ they could appoint a replacement , rather than having students vote for one . The procedures the AMS develops for appointing a replacement should address this . <h> Removing councilors <p> There is also a proposed amendment that would allow council to discipline , suspend and remove members of council ( which includes both elected councillors and AMS executives ) who are " found to be in violation of the Society 's Bylaws , Code , or internal policies . " Additionally , council can declare a member of council who has been removed from office " ineligible to be duly elected " for up to a year . <p> Clearly , this is in reaction to last year 's expulsion and removal of former VP AUA Dr ? dyn Fontana . He ran for AMS President just months after he was removed from his position as VP AUA . Current AMS President Riley Huntley was vice-chair of the committee that wrote the report that led to Fontana 's removal and ran against Fontana in this spring 's election . <p> The AMS should have a procedure to formally discipline @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with a representative who is unable to execute the duties of their office . This bylaw change provides that mechanism perfectly adequately . It also allows council to suspend an executive , rather than outright removing one , providing a less extreme course of action for minor infractions . Again , this is a positive , allowing for discipline that is less disruptive to the continuity of the union 's operations . <p> Regardless , I take solace in knowing that executive removals are nearly unheard of in our union 's history -- Fontana is the only executive to have been removed . Hopefully these new bylaws will never need to be used . <p> Resource Groups currently exist only as a provision of the AMS Code . Unlike the bylaws , code is easy to change . Only two-thirds of the 33 voting seats on council need to approve a change to the code . While resource groups are constituted under AMS Code , council could decide at any meeting that they do n't want resource groups to exist . Only 22 votes would be required to terminate them @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ AMS 's resource groups into the bylaws , creating a permanence and stability for these groups that does n't exist now . Should these bylaws go into effect , it would take another successful referendum or AGM vote to remove resource groups . In the near future , this is unlikely given the resource groups ' recent ability to drive electoral turnout . <p> Adding resource groups to the bylaws does not prevent the AMS from deconstituting a specific resource group -- as our union threatened to do to the SJC in 2024 . The change protects the concept of resource groups , not an individual resource group . Regardless , enshrining resource groups into the bylaws is valuable , ensuring that they will exist for years to come . <p> But this also comes with a notable explicit restriction on their autonomy . <p> As a subsidiary organization , the bylaws would allow council to require resource groups to seek consent to " conduct any functions or activities using the name of the University or the Society " or " conduct any fund-raising activities including any charity drives . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and constituencies , these bylaw amendments extend them to resource groups . <p> I am concerned that this provision might be used to suppress resource groups in the future . I do n't think it 's an imminent concern -- I ca n't find an instance of the AMS requiring subsidiaries to seek consent for either activity . The section of AMS Code on resource groups reads , " Neither the Clubs and Societies Committee , the Finance Committee , an Executive nor the Executive Committee shall interfere with the discharge of duties by the RGAC specified in this section . " I 'd be incredibly surprised if this was used before I graduate -- especially by the current administration . These laws were updated in 1994 through the San Remo Manual and are accepted as applicable rules for naval warfare by virtually all countries . <p> This manual states that a naval blockade can only be established in international armed conflicts , i.e. , wars between two " states . " The war between Hamas and Israel is a non-international war because Israel does not recognize Palestine or Gaza as a state . <p> The ships that are part of the Global Sumud Flotilla are under @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ they remain in international waters . According to Prime Minister Mark Carney , Canada is willing to participate in a multilateral mission to " enforce peace " in the enclave . <p> Is that a good idea ? <p> Carney 's announcement follows the New York Declaration , which calls for " the deployment of a temporary international stabilization mission " to protect Palestinian civilians , dismantle Hamas and offer security guarantees for Palestine and Israel , " including monitoring of the ceasefire and of a future peace agreement . " Point 15 of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for an " International Stabilization Force " that would be Arab-led and offer a " long-term internal security solution " for Gaza . <p> This is unprecedented territory : never before has Canada contemplated participating in a force to protect civilians from a terrorist group and an ostensible ally waging an increasingly acknowledged genocide . If it goes ahead , would intervention protect peace and Palestinians ? <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> Many Canadians are proud of the country 's role in crafting the Responsibility to Protect ( R2P ) , a doctrine that says that where a state fails to protect its people from atrocities , the international community must act . Those who support intervention often see military action as a last resort when the lives of civilians are in imminent danger -- as they are in Gaza . They know that peace requires protecting civilians , something Israel and Hamas wo n't do . Supporters are also compelled to act by past failures to protect populations , like the 1994 Rwandan Genocide and the Holocaust . <p> Others observe that ideas like R2P have always had a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ interventions may save some lives but cost many others . They likewise have a penchant for getting states mired into poorly considered nation-building projects more akin to occupation than protection or liberation . <p> By way of example , Canada may have sent troops to free Afghans from the Taliban and secure the rights of Afghan women and girls . But today the Taliban is back in power , Canada is suing Afghanistan over gender discrimination , and " cats have more freedom than women in Afghanistan . " <p> Would an intervention in Gaza look any different ? <p> Carney has left the door open to contributing " funds , material or personnel " to a force . Could that include troops ? Canada 's UN peacekeeper contributions are dismal , but Ottawa has provided personnel for previous humanitarian interventions . The 2011 NATO intervention into Libya was led by a Canadian and included Canadian air support , though no troops in Libya itself . <p> Washington has said none of its troops will enter Gaza and Israel is apprehensive , suggesting it will soon return to military operations @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ territory . <p> Still , other states are making pledges . For example , Indonesia has announced that it " is prepared to deploy 20,000 or even more of our sons and daughters to help secure peace in Gaza . " <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> Note those words : " secure the peace " ; not " keep the peace . " Carney also did not use the word " peacekeeping . " He described the possibility of enforcing peace . The former assumes there exists a peace to keep ; the latter implies troops could use force when confronted by actors who pose a threat to civilians . They wo n't just keep the peace , they 'll impose it . Given Hamas 's penchant to commit atrocities and Israel 's record of attacking peacekeepers , determining the precise mandate of the stabilization force is critical . <p> Many questions need to be answered . How far must Israel withdraw from Gaza before a force is installed ? Which Palestinian factions will a mission partner with given that the Palestinian Authority does not control @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ force against actors harming civilians ? What will its role be in securing food and humanitarian aid ? How will the force foster Palestinian self-determination rather than continued occupation ? And how long will the mission operate ? <p> Crucially , military intervention should only be available as a last resort when all other means of stopping atrocities are exhausted . In Gaza , they have n't been . States can do much more , now , before any forces are deployed : suspending trade relations with Israel , issuing sanctions , and pursuing accountability for perpetrators of atrocities in Gaza . <p> Slovenian President Nata ? a Pirc Musar was right when she recently told world leaders : " We did not stop the Holocaust , we did not stop the genocide in Rwanda , we did not stop the genocide in Srebrenica . @@130416467 <p> Donald Trump 's peace accord in the Middle East is winning as much praise , if not more , than any foreign policy triumph by a U.S. president in decades . <p> It 's like Richard Nixon going to China or Jimmy Carter 's Camp David Accords . Ronald Reagan 's role in ending the Cold War comes to mind in terms of magnitude , but that was more Mikhail Gorbachev 's doing than Mr. Reagan 's . <p> Like Mr. Trump , Mr. Reagan was a showman . In Canada , we initially feared he was a warmonger , and there was good reason - such as the time he returned from a trip to Latin America - to be concerned about his policy depth . " You 'd be surprised , " Mr. Reagan eyepoppingly observed . " They 're all individual countries . " <p> But Mr. Reagan became a peacemaker . And while there have been fears that Mr. Trump 's recklessness would lead to wars , he 's donned the mantle of peacemaker as well . <p> Much could go wrong with Mr. Trump @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ But it would be churlish not to give him his due . Political enemies are singing his praises . Even late-night liberal comics Jimmy Kimmel and Stephen Colbert are applauding . Venezuelan Mar ? a Corina Machado dedicated her Nobel Peace Prize to him . <p> A President obsessed with self-aggrandizement is getting hero worship in gushes . And therein lies the danger . The Trump success serves to vindicate and legitimize the authoritarian brand of his presidency . It provides cover for autocracy . <p> Given his taking a wrecking ball to checks and balances in the system , Mr. Trump had already come to be regarded as the most powerful of presidents . But if he was Caesar before , he is Goliath now . And woe be the consequences . <p> Having achieved peace abroad , he now has more licence to wage war at home . <p> War at home ? Where does it stop ? He is at war with the media , with anyone who has crossed him , with diversity , with Democrat-run cities to which he has dispatched the military , with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with universities , with truth , with people of colour , with free trade , with immigrants , with the deep state ( with his mass firings ) , with Congress , which is shut down . <p> There can be no expectation that Mr. Trump will back off on his extremely divisive approach , only that he will press his agenda harder . The narcissist President believed he could do no wrong . Now with so many falling at his feet , he will be convinced of it . Out of fear of harsh retribution , there were n't many who were prepared to stand up to him . Now there will be even fewer . <p> The fourth estate , the institution that can check him , is becoming more weakened by the day . The free press under Mr. Trump means one that does not criticize his administration . In an interview with Vice-President JD Vance , George Stephanopoulos of ABC asked a legitimate question about border czar Tom Homan allegedly accepting a US$50,000 bag of cash . Mr. Vance immediately took to trashing his interviewer , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reporter asked Mr. Trump a question . " I do n't take questions from ' ABC Fake News , ' " he responded , " after what you did with Stephanopoulos with the Vice-President of the United States . " <p> Foreign leaders were hardly inclined to challenge Mr. Trump before . They 'll be lining up even more to seek his favour now . Prime Minister Mark Carney quickly arranged a flight to Egypt Sunday to take part in the signing of the Gaza peace deal . Given the importance of the occasion it was the right thing to do . The two seemed to get along . In his speech , Mr. Trump accidentally referred to Mr. Carney as president instead of prime minister . " At least I did n't call you ' governor , ' " he cracked when seeing the PM later . <p> Mr. Trump 's achievement will improve his standing in Canada a bit , according to several pollsters I contacted , but certainly not enough to overcome the intense degree of animosity he has stirred here with his trade measures . " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of Ipsos , " but in Canada , his image is shaped mostly by how he treats our country . " <p> " He will get some deserved credit here for the peace deal , " said Frank Graves of Ekos . But he warned of yet more power going to Mr. Trump 's head . " The inventory of incipient fascism in the U.S. is growing daily , as is the continued acceleration of the hyper-rich away from everyone else . " <p> Autocrats , it need be said , are capable of doing good things . Goliath 's role in Gaza proves it . But being peacemaker there increases the chances of his being the opposite at home .

The sky , once filled with drones and fire , is momentarily quiet . A fragile silence hovers . But it is not peace -- it feels like the exhausted pause between waves of destruction . <p> The world calls it a " ceasefire . " It 's the brief moment when people can finally breathe -- not in relief , but in mourning . The war has stopped temporarily . The pain has not . <p> This is the moment when Gazans , after enduring unimaginable loss , are left with the unbearable task of counting the dead . They grieve for their children , their parents , their friends -- and for the pieces of themselves buried under the rubble . <p> This is when many will try to brand this tragedy as a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " of violence . But for those who have lived it , there is no symmetry in the suffering , no balance in the injustice . The truth must not be blurred . <p> Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians returned to a devastated Gaza City.BASHAR TALEB/AFP/Getty Images <p> The poet Mahmoud Darwish once wrote : " After the war , the leaders shake hands . " We saw this truth unfold again . Politicians meet , smile and declare " understandings , " while the people who have lost everything are left to face the silence of absence . <p> So let the leaders shake hands . But let the world also listen to those who carry both the memory of the dead and the hope of the living . Their pain is not a story to be pitied ; it is a mirror held up to the world 's conscience . And when we look , may we finally ask not who won the war , but who lost their humanity . <p> The cost is beyond what the world can see . It is not only the destroyed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ invisible damage that seeps into every breath , every heartbeat , every dream . The loss of hope , the disfigurement of memory , the fear that peace is impossible -- these are the wounds no ceasefire can heal . <p> Yesterday , I spoke with my brother , whose family has been displaced . I asked him when they were going to return to Gaza . He paused , then said quietly : " Where to go ? Our home is demolished , and the whole area is a ghost . Let us remain here , where we have a tent , until we see . " <p> Those heart-piercing words capture the reality of millions of Palestinians -- people suspended between past and future , between rubble and exile . My brother 's question echoes through every corner of Gaza , where families stand amid ruins , unsure whether the silence means survival or the calm before another storm . <p> That question -- where to go -- is the deepest wound of all . When people are denied not only safety but also the meaning of home @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Displacement becomes not just a physical state , but a psychological exile . <p> These uncertain times are painful and fearful , too . Will the ceasefire continue long enough to end not only the war , but also its root causes ? Those who speak of " the end of war " without addressing its causes are merely preparing for the next one . We need to understand that military means will never bring safety , security or peace -- that every bomb dropped on civilians deepens the insecurity it claims to end , and that every child killed plants the seed of future rage . <p> So we grieve . But grieving is not a weakness ; it is a moral right . It affirms that every life matters , that the dead are not numbers but names , faces , stories . But then we must transform grief into justice and accountability . <p> Gazans are not asking for pity . They are asking for life -- a life with safety , dignity and meaning . That begins with reconstruction , both physical and emotional . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ones : the broken hearts , the orphaned memories , the generations growing up surrounded by loss and yet still daring to hope . The inner architecture of peace -- education , culture , public health and the restoration of human connection , dignity and the sense that life has value -- will require patience and deeper investment to restore . And here is a silver lining : a rare opportunity for all to finally understand that the path to peace does not begin with military might , and that true reconstruction begins inside people . <p> In this moment , our world must also restore trust -- in humanity , in the rule of law and in the international organizations created to protect it . Only in a world where every life is equal and valued , and all are accountable for their actions , can peace have meaning and permanence .

@@130439197 <h> Believe , trust in beauty <p> Fyodor Dostoevsky never said or wrote the words attributed to him that " Beauty will save the world " but the thought contains such hope that it seems suited to a writer of his genius . <p> A major element of that hope is the stark counterpoint it presents to the grim daily reality of horrible ugliness that threatens the world . <p> Shadowing the beauty of the release of the Israeli hostages on Thanksgiving were the demonic acts of slaughter perpetrated by Hamas almost two years to the day before , and the squalor that awaits Palestinians as they make their way to ruined homes to mourn their own dead loved ones . <p> Advertisement <p> Amid the beautiful heroism of the Ukrainian people holding on in courage against the vicious , megalomaniacal Vladimir Putin are the spectres of slain children , mothers , fathers , people who went out to buy milk or go to work and never came back . <p> The seemingly infinite struggle between the glorious and the damnable is hardly confined to those two conflicts . Indeed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ regions where it goes on would surely exhaust most , if not all , the letters of the alphabet . <p> Paradoxically compounding the burden of living in a world fraught with such struggle is the often-staggering difficulty of heeding our own Christian faith 's call and obligation to resist giving into the despair that forges a path to the nightmare of nihilism . <p> Yet as guest columnist Leonard DeLorenzo writes on our pages this week , what the Faith asks of us , it also gives back to us as gift . He cites the case of a writer named Sarah Clarkson who went through mental health afflictions that personified the madness of our mad , mad world and overpowered them by shifting her gaze from worldly infinite struggle to God 's eternal beauty . <p> Advertisement <p> " ( Clarkson ) began practicing trusting the story of beauty , " DeLorenzo writes . <p> He quotes her words : " My deep belief is that beauty has a story to tell , one that was meant by God to speak to us of His character and reality @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ We know God when we behold His beauty , when His goodness invades the secret rooms of our hearts . To believe the truth that beauty tells : this is our great struggle from the depths of our grief . " <p> There is resonance of Clarkson 's discovery in the message Pope Leo recently delivered in Rome to members of Aid to the Church in Need where he lauded the international organization 's ceaseless struggle for religious freedom across the globe . In essence , the Holy Father said , Aid to the Church in Need is a model of the Church we need to aid in making religious freedom a watchword for the beauty of peaceful co-existence . <p> " Your assistance helps Christians , even small and vulnerable minorities , to be " peacemakers " in their homelands , " the Pontiff told delegates . " In the Central Africa Republic , Burkina Faso and Mozambique , the local Church -- often sustained by your help -- becomes a living sign of social harmony and fraternity , showing their neighbours that a different world is possible . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ free faith to promote peace , and Clarkson 's insight into the salvific gift of trusting Beauty , are no verbal pacifiers to turn our frowns upside down and let us shrug off ugliness with a dismissive " oh , it 's not so bad after all . " It is so bad . It is so ugly . The reality of our world shows it so . <p> Gaza , Ukraine , the alphabet of earth 's suffering peoples , provide the daily proof . So , and we must not shy away from this , does the Church 's own tormented struggles with the priestly sexual abuse scandals of recent decades . Let us not forget , either , our Catholic reckoning with complicity in sins against Indigenous people here in Canada . <p> Advertisement <p> But , as St. Paul might say , by no means does that negate the Beauty that goes always before us . What could be more beautiful , after all , than He who came to take away the sins of the world ? What could lift our eyes and hearts more @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ loved the world ? Yet , unbelievable as it sometimes seems , there actually is more . <p> There is the Beauty of the Mass through which we are invited to participate body , mind and spirit in His death and Resurrection . There , the secret , shadowed , ugly rooms of our human hearts can be opened to the truth whose Beauty has already saved the world . <p> A version of this story appeared in the October 19 , 2025 , issue of The Catholic Register with the headline " Believe , trust in beauty " . <p> Join the conversation and have your say : submit a letter to the Editor . Letters should be brief and must include full name , address and phone number ( street and phone number will not be published ) . Letters may be edited for length and clarity .

All 193 UN member states are bound to enforce sanctions implemented under Article 41 of the UN Charter . @@130456597 <p> Whatever your goals , it 's the struggle to get there that 's most rewarding . It 's almost as if life itself is inviting us to embrace difficulty -- not as punishment but as a design feature . It 's a robust system for growth . <p> We always learn from history , but we can not seem to overcome distractions long enough to apply that knowledge . <p> " Human nature will not change . In any future great national trial ... we shall have as weak and as strong , as silly and as wise , as bad and as good . " -- Abraham Lincoln ? <p> Throughout history , societies have accumulated incredible knowledge and wisdom . So why is it that cyclical boom-and-bust scenarios continue to plague global markets , while populism has , once again , climbed to its highest levels since the 1930 's ? Why , as Lincoln inferred , do we seem to never learn from history ? <p> As it turns out , we have learnt a lot from history . But we are too easily distracted , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ when it is most needed . <p> Let 's take a look at how we humans are hardwired to explain this unique phenomenon of distraction . The elegant neural architecture of our brains enables us to engage in a powerful acquisition of knowledge , and to also undertake complex rational thought . This is mostly achieved via the engagement of our prefrontal cortex and hippocampus . We are , as a species , fully equipped to learn . <p> However , our limbic system , the most ancient part of our brain , still acts in a dominant way , deeply prioritizing our short-term survival . It is why we constantly scan in a hypervigilant ( and often unconscious ) way for immediate threats , and why our reward circuits ( e.g. , dopamine receptors ) richly reward us when we indulge in survivalist-focused behaviors . It also explains our vulnerability to distraction , which means that often we can not engage in our rational ability to analyze at all . <p> An example : Many of us studied complex historical , political or sociological theory at college , but @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . One reason ? We are daily social media users , which is where we often now consume our news content . A fake news post we have just read triggers a tribalist , hypervigilant ( limbic system-originated ) response in us , and we type out an emotional , angry post . There is no time , space , or opportunity for rational application of the knowledge we already possess . News has become an emotional affair . <p> The prefrontal cortex ( which enables deep analysis , application of theory to current events , etc. ) simply can not compete in these situations . For a start , it can not titillate our reward circuits in the same way as a sensationalised news story can . So reading a pile of historical journals about , say , Gaza or Israel , is not going to immediately stimulate us in the way that a short , outrageous emotional online post can . The social media post leads to our brain receiving immediate gratification for our interaction ( increased oxytocin release , for example , after we see online friends @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are activated , and we are sated in some way . <p> For our caveman ancestors , hypervigilance , social bonding , and emotional reactivity were the instincts that kept us alive . But today , the need for complex , analytical , non-distracted thought has become vital . <p> Cognitive warfare image <p> Source : Elesa Zehndorfer <h> Forces That Shape ( and Shatter ) History 's Lessons <p> The landscape darkens when we consider that we are becoming more distracted than ever , with external forces ( e.g. , fake news and propaganda creators ) now actively weaponizing our survival instincts -- and vulnerability for distraction -- against us . The goal is to dissuade us from using our prefrontal cortex when engaging with news or politics , and instead remain in an emotionally reactive state . NATO refers to it as cognitive warfare , and here 's how it works : <p> Frequent use of fake news , propaganda , attack ads , and even funny memes are designed to subtly shift our relationship with news and politics from a rational to an emotionally-driven affair . Daily @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reactive , with fake posts constantly triggering our survival reflexes ( e.g. , sharing an angry post about immigrants attacking local women : we feel tribal and hypervigilant ) . Bots constantly distract us with ridiculous inflammatory statements , arguments , and language . The aim is to dominate our attention , draining our mental energy . <h> An Honest Reckoning with Human Nature ? <p> Lincoln 's words , " Human nature will not change , " is a truism . After all , we are animals , so our animal instincts can always emerge , and dominate , no matter how capable of rational analysis we might be . <p> But our generation now appears to have reached a crossroads , one where we recognize that digital media and cable TV content weaponizes our evolutionary design ( effectively ) against us . These days , the art of distraction is systematically deployed to dissuade us from the deep thinking that we are capable of . Curiously , we see the dangers and mechanics of distraction , yet still we engage . <p> Consequently , the question , " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to rest on a false premise . After all , our acquisition of knowledge over generations -- of history , science , the arts -- is demonstrably phenomenal ; in fact , it appears to be a passion for us as a species . <p> Collectively turning away from distraction , long enough to apply what we know , however ? It is a skill that we do not yet appear to have mastered . And perhaps we never will . <p> Whatever your goals , it 's the struggle to get there that 's most rewarding . It 's almost as if life itself is inviting us to embrace difficulty -- not as punishment but as a design feature . It 's a robust system for growth .

They were spoken by Progressive Conservative prime minister John Diefenbaker . Long before Pierre Trudeau enshrined our Charter of Rights and Freedoms , Diefenbaker was Canada 's champion of equality , passing the federal Bill of Rights in 1960 . <p> With Diefenbaker 's words and legacy as a backstop , we conservatives must now be brave enough to oppose what one conservative government is planning -- because while governments expect pushback from their standard political opponents , they do n't always expect it from supporters . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> ARTICLE @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ government 's plan to add a marker to driver 's licences indicating whether the holder is a Canadian citizen . @@130494081 <p> For more than 5,000 years the Gaza Strip has been a meeting point of civilizations , from the Canaanites and Pharaohs to the Romans and Ottomans , all of whom left a mark in the many monuments , archeological sites and places of worship that reflectedGaza 's proud heritage . <p> But after two years of war , many of the identifying landmarks of the armies and people who have passed through this 40-kilometre stretch of land on the Mediterranean coast are gone or in danger of disappearing . <p> Palestinians are only now taking in the full extent of the loss after Israel paused its relentless bombardment last Friday , under the terms of the Israel-Hamas ceasefire negotiated by international mediators in Egypt . As a bridge between Asia and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ attracted scholars , traders and pilgrims . By the time British took over in 1917 , Gaza was a fishing town . @@130524222 <h> Byron Blake Award and reward : Is there a difference ? <p> In an increasingly transactional , materialistic , and individualistic world , the distinction between award and reward has become blurred . Service has been replaced by " what is in it for me " and civil duty by a " payment first mentality " even good people struggle to differentiate . <p> President Donald Trump 's public campaign for the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize , our Heroes Day with the presentation of National Awards , and the perennial debate for the award of National Hero to Bob Marley and Louise Bennett have reignited the issue in my mind . <h> WHAT IS A REWARD ? <p> The Oxford Dictionary defines reward as " given in recognition of a service , effort , or achievement " It is earned . It is a right . Failure to discharge the obligation can be challenged in court or other competent forum " . <h> WHAT IS AN AWARD ? <p> The Oxford Dictionary defines an award as " giving what is deserved or merited usually after careful weighing of pertinent @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ others . There is no legal claim . Failure to award can not be litigated . <p> The qualifications for awards may be codified , but final judgment is in the eyes of those tasked with making the award . Canvassing or self-promotion is often disqualifying . <h> Headlines Delivered to Your Inbox <h> JAMAICAN HONOURS SYSTEM <p> The Jamaican honours system is rooted in the National Honours and Awards Act passed by the Parliament of Jamaica in 1969 ( Act No. 21 of 1969 ) . It recognised the Order of National Hero . The Act was modified to include Order of the Nation as the second-highest honour in 1973 , the Order of Excellence in 2003 , and the Order of Merit in 2003 . Other honours include Order of Jamaica , Order of Distinction , Badge of Honour , and Medal of Honour . <p> The governor general is the chancellor of the orders . He confers honours on the advice of the prime minister . But that advice follows a process . The public is invited to make nominations in a prescribed manner and within a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ should not be informed . The nominations are reviewed and assessed by the National Honours and Awards Committee , which makes recommendations to the prime minister . <p> Questions have been raised about particular awardees , but these have been defended by reference to the integrity of the process . An emerging practice , accepted by both sides of Parliament , could lead to legitimate questions . We refer to awards to members of parliament after a prescribed period in the House . This could lead not only to a presumption of entitlement but to persons with few accomplishments and questionable ethics receiving awards . This could reduce the prestige of awards . <p> The almost annual increase in the number of awards in each category could also lead to a weakening in the prestige of the awards . <h> AWARD OF NATIONAL HERO <p> The award of National Hero can be made to a person born in or living in Jamaica at the time of death . A " born Jamaican " can receive the award while alive . <p> Seven persons have been named to the Order . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Sir Alexander Bustamante , was recognised in 1969 . There have been intermittent , sometimes vociferous calls for others to be named to the Order . A committee established by former Prime Minister Bruce Golding did not recommend extension . This discussion is healthy and should continue . <p> We extend our congratulations to all Jamaicans who will receive their national awards on October 20 . <h> TRUMP 'S CAMPAIGN <p> Donald Trump approached his second presidency promising to end hot wars between Russia and Ukraine and in Gaza on his first day in Office . @@130552889 <p> The rough outline of loss in Gaza is easily visible from space . Eighty-four per cent of what humans built there has been destroyed . @@130623663 <h> Editorial : Whose body counts ? <p> Some bodies are visible only in crisis : when they 're detained , denied or dissected by policy . Others are celebrated until they challenge comfort . Some are flattened into headlines or hashtags , others erased entirely . The body should be personal , but it 's never just ours . It 's the first site of power , politics and perception -- the terrain where we assign value and negotiate the difference . <p> Across systems , bodies are ranked and regulated . Immigration policies decide which ones are " skilled . " Borders decide which ones can move . Workplaces decide which ones are productive . Police decide which ones are suspicious . Healthcare decides which ones are worth saving . Every institution carries a standard -- an unspoken image of the " acceptable " body -- and they punish every deviation from it in ways both loud and silent . <p> Some bodies are deemed valuable . Others are treated as disposable . <p> White bodies are protected and centred . Brown and Black bodies are policed , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ neglect -- denied adequate healthcare , justice and safety . Police continue to target minorities , their victims momentarily acknowledged before they push them out of the news cycle . Unhoused people die in the cold every winter as cities shuffle them out of sight , their suffering framed as an inconvenience instead of a failure of policy . The trans community still fights for the right to healthcare while provinces consider restricting gender-affirming care . <p> Immigrants are used as political chips , welcomed when they fill labour shortages , but left without protection when they face racism and exploitation in their workplaces and communities , and are forced to jump through hoops to obtain permanent residency . <p> In Canada , this logic plays out in both immigrant-heavy workplaces and public infrastructure . In Quebec , for instance , workers at Amazon 's warehouse network lost their jobs in May 2024 when Amazon shuttered all seven of its Quebec facilities , a move widely seen as anti-union retaliation . <p> South of the border , Immigration and ? Customs ? Enforcement ( ICE ) detention centres hold record @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ where reports of medical neglect , heat exposure and abuse against detainees continue to surface . These centres disproportionately target visible minorities , turning racialized bodies into symbols of state control . These bodies , like so many others , become bargaining tools in political games that trade humanity for headlines . <p> Disabled bodies are treated as burdens , with city designs remaining inaccessible . Fat bodies are mocked and medicalized , told to slim down to deserve care . <p> This hierarchy of worth extends globally . The ongoing genocide in Gaza has turned Palestinian men , women and children into statistics , stripped of names and context . In Sudan , mass displacement and famine are met with silence . In the Congo , children mine the minerals that power our devices , their suffering reduced to the cost of convenience . Each crisis exposes the same truth : the world has decided which bodies matter , and which can be sacrificed . <p> Even our language reveals this logic . Words like " fit , " " normal , " " passing , " " professional @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ A trans body is questioned ; a fat body is ridiculed ; a disabled body is treated as second-class . A racialized body is expected to educate others on its pain while performing resilience . A poor body is criminalized simply for existing in public space . These contradictions pile up until existence itself becomes labour . <p> Capitalism thrives on that exhaustion . On how much we can endure before collapsing . The system depends on bodies it can overwork and replace . The suffering of some becomes a political spectacle , while others are n't even valuable enough to view . When people die in shelters , detention centres or police custody , we treat them not as tragedies but as numbers , proof that some lives are simply expected to end quietly . <p> And yet , there is resistance in the body . In queerness that refuses definition . In immigrant joy that persists . In fatness that takes up space without apology . In disability that refuses pity . In transness that exists without permission . These are not side notes to survival ; they @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to confront that hierarchy head-on through our ongoing reporting . We examine the systems that decide whose lives are liveable , and remind readers that these struggles are connected . From the streets of Montreal to picket lines , from hospitals to refugee camps , from vigils to protests , the fight remains the same : every body deserves dignity . <p> Through reporting , art and testimony , The Link works to challenge the systems that decide whose stories are told -- and to amplify those too often forgotten . Because when the world treats some bodies as disposable , resistance begins with remembering they never were . <p> This article originally appeared in Volume 46 , Issue 4 , published October 21 , 2025.

As a member of the Reform Responsa Committee , I participated in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ within Jewish law and tradition . The full text of the responsum can be found here . It demonstrates that , as with many issues in Jewish law and practice , our tradition offers a pluralistic approach rather than a single solution to every problem . <p> Moreover , halakhic decisions are not static but rather evolve as new evidence is discovered . The new evidence that influenced our ruling on MAID comes from the research of Dame Cecily Saunders , who in 1967 identified the condition of " total pain , " which she defined as involving not only physical symptoms , but also " psychological , social and spiritual domains . " Dame Saunders pointed out that " as total pain increases , the patient experiences a severe loss of control over their life . " This research led us to conclude that our lives should be regarded as a covenant , a partnership with God in which we are enabled to exercise that control . <p> To bolster this conclusion , the committee cited the Talmudic passage about Rabbi Judah 's caregiver who performed an act of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ claims is contrary to Jewish law . It is a peaceful way to end suffering , often celebrating a life well lived , surrounded by loved ones , without any coercion . " <h> Other stories : <p> Hildebrand , who joined the group approximately a year ago when she retired , also has sewing and quilting as a part of her family 's history . <p> Both her grandmothers were involved in the craft , and her mother still enjoys it . <p> " I have learned from her how to scour the thrift stores for good quality sheets that are available , " she said . <h> Versatile , practical , and beautiful <p> For the pair , creating the blankets is not only a tradition that helps others but also a way to connect with the community . <p> Hildebrand said that she sometimes has blanket-making competitions with her mother ( who is usually the winner , according to her ) . <p> The group also shares fabric to create its unique comforters @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ still have the high quality that only something handmade can boast . <p> " The comforters are colourful and cozy , flannel-backed , and there 's a nice filling inside , " said Hildebrand . <p> " People have a lot of fun creating those tops at home , whether it 's from unfinished quilt projects or sheets or just good fabric that lots of women have stashes of , " added Stoesz . <p> " Comforters are so versatile that way . ( Submitted photo ) <p> Rabbi David Rotenberg got his first break performing jokes when he was 15 years old , in 1998 . He had to rush out of his yeshiva 's Talmud class to get to a 7-Eleven store payphone and book the gig at the Yuk Yuk 's comedy club in his hometown of Ottawa . <p> Over the past nearly 30 years , the Orthodox rabbi and Jewish educator chose to put his stand-up comedy career on the back burner for extended periods while he focused on his rabbinical duties and family .
